newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian cocoa bean exports down sharply in May.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian cocoa bean exports down sharply in May.

text.p: Cocoa bean exports from Ivory Coast fell to 34,966 tonnes in May, from 116,598 tonnes in April and 75,522 in May last year, according to official shipping data.
Abidjan handled 17,114 tonnes of May 1997 exports, with 17,852 leaving via the second port of San Pedro, the data show.
Cumulative exports for the first eight months of 1996/97 (Oct-Sept) totalled 918,901 tonnes, against 921,947 a year earlier.
Details of destination ports were not immediately available.

Ivory coat produced a record 1.2 million tonnes crop in 1995/96 after an unexpectedly large mid-crop (May-Sept) of 200,000 tonnes. Bean quality remained high, without the usual decrease in size as main-crops give way to mid-crops.
This year's mid-crop got off to a slow start in May and June but crop analysts expect port arrivals to pick up in July and August.
Total arrivals were about 1.05-06 million tonnes by early June, port sources said.
Exporters said bean quality for this year's mid-crop was beginning to improve after initial quality problems.
"We are getting back to 110-115 (beans per 100 grams) in some areas," a crop analyst told Reuters. That compared with 130-150 in some places in May and June.
"Some is also being set aside to carry over into 1997/98 (Oct-Sept)," he added.

Farmers and buyers usually hold around 40-70,000 tonnes of mid-crop in stock to benefit from farmgate or international price rises as mid-crop seasons give way to the following main crop. The precise amounts carried over are never clear.

"The farmgate price has been the same for three years (315 CFA a kilo). With world prices as high as they have been, I would have certainly expected a rise," said the crop analyst. That would encourage retention of stocks by farmers, he added.
Some mid-crop cocoa had also been mixed with generally better quality main crop to reach an overall export standard of 105 beans per 100 grams with a humidity of up to eight percent.
Early July weather has been dry after abnormally heavy June rains, favouring drying of beans by farmers.
